title: The Last Contract of Isako
author: Lee, Fonda
review:
4.25/5 Cyberpunk samurai Succession in Space!

I received a copy of this book on Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

I read all of Greenbone Saga a few years ago and thought it got progressively better so I was excited to read this one and see what Fonda Lee can do with a sci-fi Cyberpunk setting, really good premise and world.

The immediate hook of the book I thought was quite good and it pulled me in quickly, the character of Isako is compelling as a samurai contractor past her prime, aging, and recently failed her last big contract is the sort of protagonist we don't get often.

The mystery set up was compelling and kept me turning the pages, I was impressed with how Lee kept the scope of the story controlled where sometimes with sci-fi settings there's a tendency to go huge and epic right away which can rob the build up.

The book does a good job of focusing on the political complexities of the various factions in this world and all the competing motivations, in particular there's a number of characters that you're trying to figure out the whole book and the way she slow rolls their motivations and gray morality was very well done, there's a tendency to paint leaders as always corrupt and morally bankrupt but I think she treats the motivations of them with a lot of nuance that makes it complex and interesting to think about.

She also uses perspective in a really great way and the book turns on its head at one point that really surprised me. This was probably my favorite part and was really compelling to read, loved the tackling of this mystery from multiple angles and her challenging what we think we know.

The ending was pretty solid, think I wanted some more at certain points in the book, there's some decent ideas in the book but if you're looking for mind shattering sci-fi ideas you're probably looking in the wrong place here.

My recommendation for something similar that is one of my favorite sci-fi standalones is Chasm City by Alastair Reynolds, it has a lot more complexity and mind blowing moments. Isako is a lot more approachable and does the politics and characters better however. 

I also was a bit surprised that the action was not that prevalent being a samurai story so you might be disappointed if you're looking for that. It's more restrained there and it builds up with more personal politics and had some moments of action but nothing that jaw dropping and not much spectacle. 

Overall I really enjoyed this a lot as a character focused political Cyberpunk sci-fi story and would love to read more in this setting. I also think this is ripe for adaptation and would make a great movie/TV show/video game. Really good foundation for further exploration of this setting.
